list.query:
WITH resp AS (
  SELECT http_get(
    'https://earth-search.aws.element84.com/v1/search'
    || '?collections=sentinel-2-l2a'
    || '&bbox=-79.10,-3.05,-78.90,-2.85'
    || '&datetime=' || $__timeFrom() || '/' || $__timeTo()
    || '&limit=100'
  ) AS r
),
features AS (
  SELECT unnest(json_extract(r->>'body', '$.features[*]')) AS f FROM resp
)
SELECT f->'assets'->'red'->>'href'
FROM features
WHERE (f->'properties'->>'eo:cloud_cover')::DOUBLE < 60
ORDER BY (f->'properties'->>'datetime')::TIMESTAMP DESC
LIMIT 1

title: Raster — COG and STAC through TiTiler

options.content:
# Cloud-native raster

One query discovers the scene and the map draws it. There is no ETL and no download: DuckDB asks Sentinel-2's STAC catalogue which image covers Cuenca inside the dashboard's range, gets back **one row** with the link to the COG, and the panel hands it to TiTiler, which serves the tiles by reading the remote file over byte ranges.

The same server also knows how to **measure** what it serves, so the two panels below get numbers out of the raster without bringing a single pixel into the browser: the mean of the red band over an area, and the value of the pixel wherever you click on the map.

| Piece | Who provides it |
|---|---|
| Catalogue | `earth-search.aws.element84.com`, public and unauthenticated |
| Search | DuckDB with the `http_client` extension, parameterised by the range |
| Tiles and statistics | the compose file's `titiler` container |
| Drawing | `RasterTileLayer`, which kepler already ships |

**Move the date range**: the scene and the numbers change, the viewport does not. If no image in the period is under 60 % cloud, the query returns nothing and there is no raster to draw.

**The two panels below ask nothing over HTTP.** The zonal statistic is computed inside DuckDB, joining the raster to the table of zones — four zones or four thousand, one query. And the NDVI is computed in SQL and written as a COG, which TiTiler serves exactly like a remote scene:

```sql
COPY (
  SELECT r.geometry,
         -- NDVI (-0.2 .. 0.9) stretched over the integer's range.
         RT_Cube2TypeUInt16(((n.databand_1 - r.databand_1) / (n.databand_1 + r.databand_1)
                             + 0.2) / 1.1 * 65535.0) AS ndvi
  FROM RT_Read('/testdata/raster/cuenca-b04.tif') r
  JOIN RT_Read('/testdata/raster/cuenca-b08.tif') n ON r.id = n.id)
TO '/derived/ndvi-cuenca-u16.tif'
WITH (FORMAT RASTER, DRIVER 'COG', SRS 'EPSG:4326',
      DATABAND_COLUMNS ['ndvi'], CREATION_OPTIONS ('COMPRESS=DEFLATE'));
```

That query is **not** in any panel, and that is deliberate: it writes a file, and a dashboard refreshing every 30 s must not redo a computation each time. It is run once — from Explore, against the DuckDB datasource — and the panels read what is already there. If the NDVI panel comes up empty, nobody has run it yet.

**The integer is not a detail**: kepler will not draw a `float32` raster (the layer is simply missing, with nothing said) and `uint8` comes out as a flat sheet of colour. `uint16` is what works.

panels.description: The same query that feeds the map. Here it is raw, as the panel receives it: one row, with the raster_url column the plugin detects by name.

targets.rawSql:
WITH resp AS (
  SELECT http_get(
    'https://earth-search.aws.element84.com/v1/search'
    || '?collections=sentinel-2-l2a'
    || '&bbox=-79.10,-3.05,-78.90,-2.85'
    || '&datetime=' || $__timeFrom() || '/' || $__timeTo()
    || '&limit=100'
  ) AS r
),
features AS (
  SELECT unnest(json_extract(r->>'body', '$.features[*]')) AS f FROM resp
)
SELECT
  f->>'id'                                     AS scene_id,
  (f->'properties'->>'datetime')::TIMESTAMP    AS acquired,
  (f->'properties'->>'eo:cloud_cover')::DOUBLE AS cloud_cover,
  f->'assets'->'visual'->>'href'               AS raster_url
FROM features
WHERE (f->'properties'->>'eo:cloud_cover')::DOUBLE < 60
ORDER BY acquired DESC
LIMIT 1

panels.description: RT_CubeClip + RT_CubeStats_Agg with GROUP BY: one row per zone, joined to the population already living in the table. Four zones or four thousand, it is the same query.

targets.rawSql:
-- Estadística zonal dentro de la base de datos: el ráster se une a tus
-- propias tablas en SQL, en una sola consulta, en vez de una petición HTTP
-- por zona. Es lo que un servidor de teselas no puede hacer.
LOAD raster; LOAD spatial;
WITH zonas AS (
  SELECT name, population, geometry AS geom
  FROM read_parquet('/testdata/cuenca-zones.parquet')
),
teselas AS (
  SELECT geometry, tile_x, tile_y, metadata, databand_1 AS band
  FROM RT_Read('/testdata/raster/cuenca-b04.tif')
),
recortes AS (
  -- El recorte rellena con 0 fuera del polígono; declararlo nodata es lo que
  -- impide que ese relleno entre en la media.
  SELECT z.name, z.population,
         RT_CubeSetNoData(RT_CubeClip(t.band, t.tile_x, t.tile_y, t.metadata, z.geom, 0.0), 0.0) AS cube
  FROM teselas t JOIN zonas z ON ST_Intersects(t.geometry, z.geom)
)
SELECT name AS zona,
       round((RT_CubeStats_Agg(cube, 0)).mean, 1)   AS reflectancia_media,
       (RT_CubeStats_Agg(cube, 0)).valid_count      AS pixeles,
       (RT_CubeStats_Agg(cube, 0)).minimum          AS minimo,
       (RT_CubeStats_Agg(cube, 0)).maximum          AS maximo,
       population                                   AS poblacion
FROM recortes
GROUP BY name, population
ORDER BY reflectancia_media DESC
